chapters.title: Chapter 3: Working Capital Policy and Requirement

lessons.title: Estimating How Much Working Capital a Business Needs

children.text: A promoter tells his banker he needs another ₹15 crore of working capital limit. The banker asks how he arrived at ₹15 crore. He says it feels about right, given how tight things have been. That conversation ends badly, and it ends badly every time.

There are three ways to estimate a working capital requirement properly. Two take a few minutes and give you a range. The third takes an afternoon, gives you a defensible number, and is the one your bank will ask for anyway.
Method One: Percentage of Sales

The fastest method assumes the business will keep locking up the same share of sales as it does today. Sagar Castings Ltd, a mid-sized foundry, did ₹180 crore of sales last year with ₹53.5 crore of operating working capital, and projects ₹240 crore next year, growth of about 33%.

body.caption: Percentage of sales: quick, and only as good as the assumption that nothing changes

children.text: Working capital is 29.72% of current sales, so the projection is ₹240 crore times 29.72%, which is about ₹71.33 crore. Use this for a board discussion or a first sanity check, never for a bank submission. It quietly assumes the cycle stays exactly where it is, including whatever inefficiency is already baked in.
Method Two: The Operating Cycle
The second method uses the cycle you already know how to compute. Sagar Castings has an operating cycle of about 118 days of sales locked in the business.

body.caption: Operating cycle method: ties the estimate to the measured cycle

children.text: That gives ₹240 crore divided by 365, multiplied by 118 days, which is about ₹77.59 crore. Better than the first method, because you can now run the calculation again with a target cycle rather than the current one and see what a 10-day improvement is worth.
Method Three: The Detailed Build-Up
The third method estimates each component from its own
holding period

, which is how Indian banks assess a limit and how any serious internal plan should be built. Here are the assumptions for Sagar Castings next year: raw material consumed ₹132 crore, cost of goods sold ₹168 crore, so conversion cost, meaning labour, power and factory overhead, is ₹36 crore.

markDefs.definition: The number of days or months of cost a business keeps tied up in a particular item, such as 1.5 months of raw material consumption held as stock.

body.caption: Working capital requirement, built component by component (₹ crore)

cells: Full raw material plus 50% of conversion cost
Prepaid expenses, advances, GST input credit
Cushion for delays and demand swings

body.text: Notice the work in progress line. It carries the full raw material cost, because the steel is already in the casting, but only half the conversion cost, because the job is only half processed. Getting this right matters in businesses with long production cycles, and getting it wrong is the most common error in a first attempt.

body.label: Assessed requirement for FY2027
body.context: Of which the promoter contributes ₹16.47 crore as margin at 25%, and bank finance covers about ₹49.42 crore under the traditional norms from Chapter 2.

body.title: Change one assumption
body.prompt: Using the Sagar Castings build-up, suppose collections improve so that trade receivables fall from 2 months of sales to 1.5 months. Everything else stays the same. What is the net working capital requirement in ₹ crore, before the safety margin?
body.explanation: Receivables fall from ₹40 crore to ₹30 crore, so current assets drop from ₹80.75 crore to ₹70.75 crore. Subtract current liabilities of ₹18 crore and the requirement is ₹52.75 crore, a saving of ₹10 crore. Half a month of collection is worth more than most cost-cutting exercises.

children.text: Three Answers, One Decision

body.title: The same business, three estimation methods (₹ crore)

children.text: Three methods, three answers, from ₹65.89 crore to ₹77.59 crore. That spread is not a problem, it is information. The two quick methods project today's behaviour forward, while the build-up uses the holding periods the business intends to run next year. The build-up is lower because its assumptions are tighter than current performance.

columns.label: The quick methods
points: Percentage of sales and the operating cycle method
Minutes of work, using figures you already have
Good for a first sanity check or a board discussion
They project current inefficiency into next year unchanged
Useless as a defence of a limit request, because no assumption is visible

columns.label: The detailed build-up
points: Each component estimated from its own holding period
Takes real work and needs operating inputs, not just accounting ones
Required for any bank limit application
Every assumption is explicit, so each can be challenged and improved
Doubles as an operating plan: the holding periods become targets

body.text: If your detailed build-up differs sharply from the quick methods, do not just pick the answer you like. Find the assumption causing the gap. Usually it is a holding period the plan has quietly tightened without anyone deciding how it will actually be achieved.

body.title: What your banker will actually ask for

children.text: For a working capital limit, Indian banks ask for
CMA data

, a standard set of statements covering the last two or three years of actuals, the current year estimate and the following year projection, along with a working capital assessment built exactly like the table above.

markDefs.definition: Credit Monitoring Arrangement data. The standard set of forms Indian banks ask a borrower to submit, covering past and projected financials and a working capital assessment.

children.text: Two things trip up first-time applicants. The first is the
margin

: the bank funds a portion of the assessed requirement and expects the borrower to fund the rest from long-term sources. If you cannot show where the margin comes from, the limit gets cut to what your margin supports.

markDefs.definition: The borrower's own contribution to working capital, which the bank will not fund. Usually 25% of the assessed requirement under the traditional norms.

children.text: The second is consistency. The sales growth in your projection has to match the capacity you have, the holding periods have to match what your past stock statements show, and the profit has to be enough to service the facility. A projection that assumes both faster growth and a suddenly shorter cycle, with no explanation of how, invites the credit officer to apply their own numbers instead. Chapter 6 covers the assessment methods and drawing power in detail.
The Number That Matters Most

The total requirement tells you how big the operating block will be. What actually has to be arranged is the increase. Sagar Castings needs ₹65.89 crore next year against ₹53.5 crore today, so the incremental funding need is about ₹12.39 crore.

stats.label: Total requirement
stats.context: The size of the operating block at ₹240 crore of sales

stats.label: Already funded
stats.context: The working capital the business runs today

stats.label: To be arranged
stats.context: The only number that requires a decision this year

children.text: Now check whether the business can self-fund that. At a 12% operating margin on ₹240 crore, with roughly 60% of profit left after tax, interest and dividends, retained profit is about ₹17.28 crore. That comfortably covers the ₹12.39 crore of incremental working capital, with something left for capital expenditure. Run the same arithmetic at 60% growth instead of 33%, and the answer flips: the increment outruns the profit, and the business has to raise money or slow down.

body.title: The line that catches people out
body.textWithBlank: In a detailed working capital estimate, work in progress carries the full cost of raw material but only a part of the ___ cost, because the job is only partly processed.
body.explanation: Conversion cost means labour, power and factory overhead. Assuming work in progress carries either none or all of it is the most common error in a first build-up.

body.title: Which method for which purpose?
body.question: A company is applying to its bank to increase its cash credit limit ahead of a 40% growth year. Which estimation approach should form the basis of the application?
options: Percentage of sales, because it is quick and uses actual historical behaviour
The detailed component build-up, because every holding period assumption is explicit and can be defended
Last year's limit plus 40%, matching the sales growth
The operating cycle method, because it uses the measured cash conversion cycle
body.explanation: Banks assess limits from a component build-up and will ask for CMA data. The quick methods are useful as cross-checks, and scaling last year's limit by the growth rate assumes the current limit was correctly sized in the first place, which is exactly what the bank is testing.

body.title: The projection that does not add up
body.scenario: A promoter shows you a working capital estimate for next year. Sales are projected to grow from ₹90 crore to ₹150 crore. The build-up assumes raw material holding falls from 2 months to 1 month, finished goods from 1.5 months to 1 month, and receivables from 75 days to 50 days. On those assumptions the working capital requirement barely rises, so the promoter concludes no additional limit is needed.
body.prompt: What is wrong with this estimate, and how would you rework it?
body.modelAnswer:
Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic. Everything is wrong with the assumptions.

The projection has 67% sales growth arriving at the same time as a sweeping improvement in every single holding period, with no stated reason for either. Growing that fast usually stretches the cycle rather than tightening it: new customers get longer credit, wider product range means more stock keeping units, and a strained supply chain forces bigger raw material buffers. Assuming the opposite on all four lines at once is not a plan, it is a wish.

How to rework it. First, build the base case with holding periods unchanged from last year, which shows the honest funding gap at ₹150 crore of sales. Second, build a target case with improvements only where there is a specific action behind them, for example 10 fewer days of receivables backed by a named collection process and a revised credit policy. Third, show the gap between the two, and treat that gap as the value of the improvement programme rather than as funding you already have.

Then ask the question the estimate is avoiding: if none of the improvements land, can the business fund ₹150 crore of sales at last year's cycle? If the answer is no, the growth plan needs funding or the growth rate needs cutting. Better to discover that in a spreadsheet than in October.

body.title: Build your own working capital estimate
steps: Start from a sales projection you can defend, with the capacity and order book to support it.
Break next year's cost structure into raw material consumed, conversion cost and cost of goods sold.
Set a holding period for each component: raw material, work in progress, finished goods and receivables.
Base each holding period on your own last two years of actuals, adjusted only where a specific action justifies a change.
Remember that work in progress carries full raw material cost and only part of the conversion cost.
Deduct the credit you genuinely get from suppliers and the expenses that stay outstanding.
Add a safety margin of about 5% to 10% for demand swings and payment delays.
Subtract the working capital you already have funded, and treat the difference as the amount to arrange.
Cross-check the total against the percentage of sales and operating cycle methods, and investigate any wide gap.

body.text: An estimate is only as good as its holding periods. Each one is an operating commitment, so anyone who tightens an assumption in a spreadsheet must also name the person who will deliver it in the factory or the collections team.

points: Three methods exist: percentage of sales, the operating cycle method, and the detailed component build-up.
The quick methods project current behaviour forward and are useful only as sanity checks.
The detailed build-up estimates each component from its own holding period and is what banks require as part of CMA data.
Work in progress carries the full raw material cost but only a portion of the conversion cost.
Deduct supplier credit and outstanding expenses, then add a safety margin of about 5% to 10%.
The number that needs a decision is the increment over what is already funded, not the total requirement.
Compare the increment with expected retained profit to see whether growth is self-funding or needs new money.
